name: Chlorpromazine
summary: Older 'typical' antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, severe agitation, bipolar mania, intractable hiccups, and hard-to-treat nausea. Effective but carries high risk of side effects like drowsiness, movement problems, weight gain, and heart rhythm changes.
description: Chlorpromazine is one of the earliest antipsychotic medicines. It can calm severe agitation, treat psychosis, and help with stubborn nausea, vomiting, or hiccups when other options fail. However, it has a high side-effect burden, including strong sedation, low blood pressure, movement disorders, weight gain, and possible heart rhythm changes. Modern antipsychotics are usually preferred, and chlorpromazine is generally reserved for specific situations under close monitoring.
patient_summary: Chlorpromazine is an older antipsychotic that can be very helpful for severe agitation, psychosis, hard-to-treat nausea, or nonstop hiccups. It often makes people very sleepy at first and can cause dizziness when standing, weight gain, and muscle stiffness or tremors. It also carries heart and liver risks, especially at higher doses or in older adults. Because of this, doctors generally try newer options first and use chlorpromazine when the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.

primary_indications: Severe agitation or aggression related to psychosis or mania
Severe nausea and vomiting when other treatments fail

linked_conditions.context: Effective for hallucinations and delusions, but generally not first- or second-line today due to high risk of sedation, movement disorders, and metabolic side effects.
Can help control acute manic symptoms when newer antipsychotics or mood stabilizers are unavailable or poorly tolerated.
Used IM/IV in some emergency settings for severe agitation when other options are not available or appropriate.
A classic option for stubborn hiccups that haven’t responded to simpler measures.
Sometimes used for severe, short-term nausea and vomiting, including in pregnancy when supervised by specialists and other options have failed.

contraindications: Allergy to chlorpromazine or other phenothiazines
Coma or severe central nervous system depression
Concurrent use with large amounts of alcohol or other strong sedatives (eg, barbiturates, opioids)
History of severe reaction to phenothiazines (eg, jaundice or severe blood problems)
Uncontrolled severe heart disease or serious heart rhythm disorders
Possible Reye syndrome in children or teens (avoid)

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed by mouth, but a significant amount is broken down on first pass through the gut and liver.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Around one-third of the swallowed dose reaches the bloodstream unchanged.
pharmacokinetics.onset: For nausea and agitation, improvement may start within 30–60 minutes after oral or parenteral dosing. For psychosis or mania, meaningful improvement often appears over 1–2 weeks.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Typically within 2–4 hours after an oral dose.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Initial distribution half-life about 2 hours; terminal elimination around 30 hours in adults.
pharmacokinetics.duration: Single oral doses usually have noticeable effects for 4–6 hours, though some effects (like sedation and movement symptoms) can last longer.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively broken down in the liver into multiple active and inactive metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Mostly excreted in the urine as metabolites; only a very small amount leaves the body unchanged.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Highly protein bound (over 90%), which contributes to a long duration in the body.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food doesn’t dramatically change overall exposure, but may slow or smooth absorption and can help reduce stomach upset.

sections.heading: Black Box Warning: Older Adults with Dementia
sections.text: Antipsychotic drugs, including chlorpromazine, increase the risk of death in older adults with behavior problems related to dementia. Most deaths are due to heart-related problems or infections like pneumonia. Chlorpromazine is not approved to treat dementia-related behavior changes. In these situations, non-medication approaches are preferred whenever possible, and any antipsychotic use should be short-term and closely monitored.

sections.heading: What Chlorpromazine Is Used For
sections.text: Chlorpromazine is an older, broad-acting antipsychotic. Because of its side effects, it’s usually not a first choice today, but it still has important uses in specific situations.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders}: helps reduce hallucinations, delusions, and severe disorganization.
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar disorder – acute mania}: can calm extreme energy, racing thoughts, and risky behavior.
Severe agitation or aggression: especially when driven by psychosis or mania and other medicines are not available or have failed.
Prolonged or intractable hiccups: often used when simple physical maneuvers or other medications haven’t worked.
Severe short-term nausea and vomiting: including after surgery, chemotherapy, or in pregnancy (always under specialist supervision).
Adjunct in tetanus: used as one part of a larger intensive care treatment plan.
off_label: Acute migraine treatment in emergency settings (IV use in some hospitals)
Refractory nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (when other treatments have failed and benefits clearly outweigh risks)

sections.heading: What People Commonly Feel
sections.intro: Experiences vary a lot depending on dose, route (pill vs injection), and why it’s being used. These are common themes people report:

quotes: “It knocked me out at first—I was really sleepy for a few days.”
“The voices were quieter, but I felt slow and heavy.”
“It calmed the agitation, but I mostly wanted to lie down.”
“Standing up too fast made me feel like I was going to faint.”
“I got lightheaded and had to move slowly, especially in the morning.”
“My muscles felt stiff and my hands shook a bit.”
“I felt restless—like I had to keep moving my legs.”
items.note: These can be signs of movement side effects (extrapyramidal symptoms) and should always be reported to a prescriber.

quotes: “I started gaining weight after a few months.”
“My appetite went up and it was hard to control snacking.”

sections.heading: How Fast It Works and How Long It Lasts
sections.text: Chlorpromazine has both fast and slow effects, depending on what you’re treating.
key_points: Nausea, vomiting, or hiccups: Some relief can appear within 30–60 minutes after a dose (faster with IV or IM use).
Severe agitation: Calming effects may develop within an hour of injection in emergency settings.
Psychosis and mania: Initial improvements can appear within a few days, but full benefit often takes 1–2 weeks or longer.
Single oral dose: Noticeable effects generally last 4–6 hours, though drowsiness may last longer.
Long half-life: The drug and its metabolites stay in the body for many hours, so side effects can linger even after stopping.

sections.heading: Major Safety Warnings
sections.highlight: Effective but high side-effect burden—especially for movement problems, blood pressure drops, metabolic changes, and heart rhythm issues.
sections.black_box: Older adults with dementia-related behavior problems are at higher risk of death with antipsychotics, including chlorpromazine. This medicine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
other: Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): At higher doses or in people with heart disease or low potassium/magnesium, chlorpromazine can disturb heart rhythm and, in rare cases, cause a dangerous arrhythmia.
Movement disorders: Stiffness, tremors, restlessness, and long-term involuntary movements (tardive dyskinesia) are more common than with newer antipsychotics.
Severe muscle and fever reaction (Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome): A rare but life-threatening reaction with high fever, rigid muscles, confusion, and unstable blood pressure.
Blood pressure drops: Especially when standing up or after injections—can cause fainting and falls.
Liver injury: Can cause cholestatic jaundice (yellowing skin/eyes, dark urine, pale stools); sometimes serious.
Metabolic effects: Weight gain, higher blood sugar, and cholesterol changes can occur and may increase heart and diabetes risk over time.
Seizures: At higher doses or in people with seizure risk, chlorpromazine can lower the seizure threshold.
Skin and eye effects: Sun sensitivity, skin discoloration with long-term high doses, and corneal or lens deposits that can affect vision.
patient_counseling: Tell your doctor immediately if you develop yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, or severe fatigue.
Report any new or unusual muscle stiffness, shaking, tongue or facial movements, or feeling like you can’t sit still.
Stand up slowly from sitting or lying positions to reduce dizziness and fainting.
Use sunscreen and protective clothing—your skin may burn more easily in the sun.
Tell your provider about any history of heart problems, fainting, or abnormal heart rhythms.
Never stop chlorpromazine suddenly without medical guidance, especially if you’ve been on it for a long time.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Chlorpromazine is effective but has a relatively high rate of side effects, especially sedation, movement problems, and metabolic changes.
plain_language_list: Dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision
Weight gain and possible changes in blood sugar and cholesterol
Changes in menstrual periods or breast enlargement due to higher prolactin

common.incidence: Very common, especially early in treatment or at higher doses
common.patient_note: You may feel very sleepy or "slowed down." This sometimes improves after a week or two, but some grogginess can persist. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you.

common.symptom: Orthostatic Hypotension (Drop in Blood Pressure When Standing)
common.incidence: Common, especially with IM/IV dosing or in older adults
common.patient_note: You might feel lightheaded or faint when standing up. Standing slowly, staying hydrated, and reporting severe dizziness can help reduce risk of falls.

common.incidence: Common, especially at higher doses and with long-term use
common.patient_note: These can look like stiffness, tremors (similar to Parkinson’s), inner restlessness (can’t sit still), or sudden neck or eye muscle spasms. Tell your provider immediately—doses can be adjusted or other medicines added to help.

You may notice increased appetite and weight gain over time. Your provider may check your weight, blood sugar, and cholesterol and may recommend diet, activity, or a medication change if things worsen.

Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and trouble urinating can occur. Drinking water, chewing sugar-free gum, and using stool softeners or fiber may help. Severe or sudden problems urinating should be treated as urgent.

serious: Tardive dyskinesia: Long-term, often irreversible involuntary movements (especially of the face, tongue, or limbs). Risk increases with age, duration of treatment, and total dose.
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: High fever, rigid muscles, confusion, fast heart rate, sweating, and unstable blood pressure. This is a medical emergency.
Severe liver injury: Jaundice, intense fatigue, fever, or abdominal pain—requires urgent evaluation and usually permanent discontinuation.
Serious blood disorders: Very low white blood counts (infections), low platelets (bleeding), or anemia (severe fatigue, pale skin).
Dangerous heart rhythm changes: Palpitations, fainting, or sudden collapse could signal a serious arrhythmia.
Seizures: New-onset seizures or major changes in seizure pattern in those with epilepsy.

sections.heading: Important Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Chlorpromazine affects the brain, heart, and liver, so interactions are common.

items.with: Alcohol and other sedatives (benzodiazepines, sleep medicines, opioids, some antihistamines, muscle relaxants)
items.risk: Stronger sedation, confusion, slow breathing, higher fall risk, and possible overdose.
items.action: Avoid alcohol entirely. Use other sedating medicines only if your prescriber knows you are on chlorpromazine and agrees it’s necessary.

items.with: Other antipsychotics or dopamine-blocking drugs (eg, metoclopramide)
items.risk: Higher risk of movement disorders and possibly Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome.
items.action: Use with caution. Usually avoid stacking multiple dopamine-blocking drugs unless clearly needed and closely supervised.

items.with: Medicines that prolong the QT interval (many antiarrhythmics, some antibiotics, some antidepressants)
items.risk: Increased risk of dangerous heart rhythm changes.
items.action: Your provider may avoid this combination, lower doses, and/or monitor your heart with ECGs.

items.risk: Stronger drops in blood pressure, dizziness, and fainting.
items.action: Blood pressure may need closer monitoring and possible dose adjustments.

items.with: Other anticholinergic drugs (such as some bladder medicines, antihistamines, or antidepressants)
items.risk: More dry mouth, constipation, confusion, and urinary retention, especially in older adults.
items.action: Use cautiously; watch for worsening side effects and contact your provider if they become problematic.

sections.heading: Dosing Basics (Adults – Simplified Overview)
sections.text: Exact dosing is very individualized. Doctors start low and increase slowly based on response and side effects.

adult.schizophrenia_psychosis: Often started around 25–100 mg per day in divided doses, then gradually increased. Many patients fall somewhere between 200–800 mg per day. Higher doses increase side-effect risk and are rarely needed.
adult.bipolar_mania: Doses similar to those used for schizophrenia; often combined with mood stabilizers.
adult.severe_agitation_emergency: An injection of 25 mg may be given, sometimes repeated under monitoring. Switched to oral treatment as soon as possible.
adult.intractable_hiccups: Typical starting oral dose is 25 mg three or four times daily, then adjusted based on effect and tolerability.
adult.severe_nausea_vomiting: Oral or injectable doses in the 10–25 mg range every 4–6 hours may be used short-term.
adult.older_adults: Lower starting doses (eg, 10–25 mg two or three times daily) are used, and increases are made very cautiously.

sections.simple_explanation: Doctors usually begin with a small dose to see how you respond, especially because of sedation, dizziness, and movement side effects. Doses are slowly adjusted to the lowest amount that controls symptoms.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Children, and Older Adults
sections.text: Chlorpromazine can be used in certain special groups, but only when benefits clearly outweigh risks and with close monitoring.
sections.pregnancy: Chlorpromazine crosses the placenta. Most studies of related antipsychotics do not show a strong overall pattern of birth defects, but data for individual drugs are limited. Use late in pregnancy may cause newborns to be stiff, floppy, or unusually sleepy, and sometimes they can have withdrawal-like symptoms. Decisions about use in pregnancy should be made together with a psychiatrist and obstetric provider, weighing the risks of untreated illness versus medication.
sections.lactation: Chlorpromazine passes into breast milk. Some breastfed infants exposed to antipsychotics have had drowsiness, poor feeding, or delayed development, though other factors may also play a role. If used while breastfeeding, infants should be watched for unusual sleepiness, feeding problems, or poor weight gain. In some cases, switching medicines or formula-feeding may be recommended.
sections.pediatrics: Chlorpromazine has been used in children for severe behavior problems, nausea, and other conditions, but it is on pediatric "high-risk" lists because of movement disorders and hormone changes. Whenever possible, safer and more modern options are preferred. If used, doses are based on weight and children must be monitored closely.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more sensitive to sedation, confusion, blood pressure drops, falls, and movement side effects. They also have a higher baseline risk of stroke and death with antipsychotics, especially if they have dementia. If chlorpromazine must be used, doctors typically start with very low doses, increase slowly, and reassess frequently.

sections.heading: Monitoring and Follow-Up
items: Weight, blood pressure, and pulse, especially after starting or changing the dose.
Blood tests: liver function, blood counts, blood sugar, and cholesterol—especially with long-term use.
Heart rhythm (ECG), particularly if you have heart disease, are on other QT-prolonging drugs, or are taking higher doses.
Movement checks: watching for stiffness, shakes, restlessness, or unusual mouth/tongue movements.
Eye checks: for people on long-term higher doses, especially if they notice vision changes.
Mental health symptoms: tracking whether psychosis, mania, nausea, or hiccups are improving and whether side effects are tolerable.

sections.heading: Available Forms
sections.text: Chlorpromazine comes in several forms so it can be used in both hospital and outpatient settings.
items: Tablets (oral): Common strengths include 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, and 200 mg.
Oral solution / concentrate: Liquid forms that can be mixed with beverages or soft food.
Injection (IM, IV): Used in hospitals or emergency departments for severe agitation, persistent hiccups, or severe nausea.

sections.heading: How Chlorpromazine Works
sections.text: Chlorpromazine mainly works by blocking dopamine receptors in the brain. Dopamine is a signaling chemical involved in mood, movement, and perception. Blocking excess dopamine activity can reduce hallucinations, delusions, and severe agitation. The drug also affects other systems (like histamine, alpha-adrenergic, and muscarinic receptors), which explains both its benefits (anti-nausea, calming) and many of its side effects (sedation, low blood pressure, dry mouth, constipation).

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Modern Treatment
sections.text:
Chlorpromazine was a groundbreaking antipsychotic when first introduced and opened the door to modern psychiatric treatment. Today, it has largely been replaced by newer antipsychotics that usually cause fewer movement and metabolic side effects. It is now used mainly when:

- Newer antipsychotics are unavailable or not tolerated.
- A broad-acting drug is needed urgently for severe agitation or psychosis.
- Specific problems like intractable hiccups or severe nausea haven’t responded to safer options.

Because of its side-effect burden, careful monitoring and regular re-evaluation are essential.

seo.title: Chlorpromazine: Uses, Side Effects, Dosing, and Safety
seo.description: Chlorpromazine is an older antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, severe agitation, hard-to-treat nausea, and intractable hiccups. Learn how it works, common side effects, and key safety warnings in plain language.

editorial.reviewStatement: Draft educational content based on standard clinical references and safety summaries. Not a substitute for individual medical advice.

faqs.a: Chlorpromazine is an older antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, acute manic episodes in bipolar disorder, severe agitation, stubborn hiccups, and severe nausea or vomiting when other medications haven’t worked. Because of its side effects, newer antipsychotics are usually tried first for long-term treatment.

It’s much less common than it used to be. Many doctors now prefer newer antipsychotics with fewer movement and metabolic side effects. Chlorpromazine is still used in some hospitals and clinics for specific situations—like severe agitation, intractable hiccups, or refractory nausea—when its benefits outweigh its risks.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are strong drowsiness, dizziness (especially when standing up), dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, weight gain, and muscle stiffness or tremors. These are often dose-related and may improve if the dose is lowered or the medicine is changed.

faqs.q: Can chlorpromazine cause long-term movement problems?
faqs.a: Yes. With long-term use, chlorpromazine can cause tardive dyskinesia, a condition involving involuntary movements of the face, tongue, or limbs. This can sometimes be permanent, even after stopping the drug. The risk is higher in older adults and increases with higher doses and longer duration of treatment. This is one reason modern antipsychotics are often preferred.

It can. Chlorpromazine is associated with weight gain and changes in blood sugar and cholesterol, especially with ongoing use. Your provider may monitor your weight and labs and may recommend lifestyle changes or a different medicine if needed.

faqs.q: Is chlorpromazine safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Older adults are more sensitive to its side effects—especially sedation, confusion, blood pressure drops, and falls. Antipsychotics in general are linked to a higher risk of stroke and death in older adults with dementia. Because of this, chlorpromazine is usually avoided or used at very low doses with close monitoring in older patients.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking chlorpromazine?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol increases drowsiness, confusion, and the risk of dangerously low blood pressure and breathing problems. It also makes falls and accidents more likely. It’s safest to avoid alcohol completely while taking this medication.

faqs.q: How long does chlorpromazine take to work for psychosis?
faqs.a: For nausea, vomiting, or hiccups, you may notice improvement within an hour. For psychotic symptoms like hallucinations or delusions, it often takes several days to start seeing meaningful changes, and full benefit may take 1–2 weeks or longer. Your dose may be adjusted over time based on how you respond and what side effects you experience.

faqs.q: What should I do if I get very stiff, confused, and feverish on chlorpromazine?
faqs.a: These could be signs of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome, a rare but life-threatening reaction. Go to the emergency room or call emergency services immediately. Do not wait for symptoms to pass on their own.

You should not stop suddenly unless your doctor tells you to. Stopping abruptly can cause a return of symptoms and, in some cases, withdrawal-like effects (such as nausea, insomnia, or agitation). Your provider will usually reduce your dose gradually to make stopping safer and more comfortable.
